To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) customer service representatives who are treated unjustly by customers retaliate by sabotaging their customers and (2) the extent to which customer service representatives engage in customer-directed sabotage depends on the extent to which they identify with their moral self-concept.

employees who are more strongly committed to their role as a customer service representative (high in symbolization) and who are less strongly committed to the values that underlie this role (low in internalization) are more likely to engage in customer-directed retaliation when they perceive mistreatment from customers.

(a) employee mistreatment from customers relates positively with customer-directed sabotage, and that this association is stronger among employees with a strong moral identity, but only if they are low in internalization, (b) employee sabotage relates negatively to job performance.

The main takeaway from our work is that

customer service employees are more prone to sabotage customers who mistreat them than they are to sabotage co-workers who mistreat them, and that moral identity can be a protective factor for customer service employees who are exposed to interpersonal injustice.
customer mistreatment can have serious consequences for the organization, and managers should be mindful that customer-directed retaliation may occur even in cases of relatively minor mistreatment.
customer service representatives are not immune from retaliating against customers.
